cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The Catedral Metropolitana stands on the soft lakebed of Lake Texcoco, so it has sunk unevenly and parts of it lean. In the 1990s, engineers carefully removed soil from under the higher parts to even it out.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In Mexico City, a quick breakfast is often a guajolota: a tamal tucked inside a bolillo, the crusty white roll. It is cheap, heavy and filling, and often comes with a cup of warm, thick atole.

cards.headline: About this chocolate mill
cards.note: At a chocolate mill in Oaxaca, cacao is ground fresh with sugar and cinnamon, often almonds too, and each customer asks for the mix they like. The paste is pressed into tablets to take home.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Before a barrio fiesta, a calenda winds through the streets: a procession with a brass band, dancing, and big paper-and-cane puppets that people carry. The whole neighborhood helps prepare it, so the fiesta belongs to the neighbors.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Every 12 October, the image of the Virgen de Zapopan is carried from the Cathedral to her basilica in Zapopan. Huge crowds walk the route, and many go each year to keep a promise or follow a family habit.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Guadalajara has two big football teams: Chivas, in red and white, and Atlas, in red and black. In 2021 Atlas won the league title after waiting about seventy years, and many fans cried in the streets and in the cantinas.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In Guadalajara, a torta ahogada is a roll filled with meat and drowned in salsa. It's made with birote salado, a roll with a hard crust and dense crumb that keeps its shape under the sauce.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: Café de olla is coffee brewed with cinnamon and piloncillo, unrefined cane sugar, in a clay pot. The clay keeps the heat and gives the drink a slightly earthy taste.

cards.headline: About this art centre
cards.note: This art centre was a textile factory where cotton cloth was woven for decades. Its big halls, built for looms, are now studios, galleries and design shops, with high ceilings and plenty of light.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: San Miguel and nearby Dolores Hidalgo each claim to be the cradle of independence. San Miguel says Allende and the plotters were from here; Dolores says the Grito was given there. Old men enjoy this friendly argument in the park.

cards.headline: About this market stall
cards.note: A cemita poblana is named for its sesame-seed roll. What makes it a cemita is pápalo, a strong-tasting herb added fresh and raw. Some people love it, others ask for it on the side.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Puebla and Oaxaca both take great pride in their moles, and people from each place will happily argue theirs is better. Mole poblano is a dark, rich sauce of dried chiles, chocolate, spices and sesame seeds.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Every 5 May, Puebla holds a parade for its 1862 victory over a French force. The French took the city a year later, yet locals still celebrate it as their own history.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: Talavera is hand-painted tin-glazed pottery that Puebla has made since colonial times. Real Talavera from Puebla and nearby Tlaxcala has an official designation of origin and is made by hand. A café cup may be local craftwork.

cards.headline: About this fonda
cards.note: A fonda is a small place, often run by a family, that serves the day's home cooking at a fair price. Many people eat there at midday, and many Mexicans say the best food is at the fonda.

cards.headline: About this fonda
cards.note: A fonda serves the comida corrida, a set lunch from about one to five, when Mexicans eat their main meal. One price brings soup, rice or pasta, a guisado with tortillas, and an agua fresca.

cards.headline: About this tlayuda grill
cards.note: Before corn becomes masa, it is soaked and cooked with cal, lime. This is called nixtamalización. The lime loosens the kernel's tough skin, so the dough holds together for tlayudas, and it frees niacin, a B vitamin.

cards.headline: About this mezcalería
cards.note: Mezcal is made from the agave's heart, the piña, cooked slowly, traditionally in a pit in the ground. That gives it its smoky taste. Most mezcal comes from Oaxaca, and the name is protected by law.

cards.note: Día de Muertos is celebrated with ofrendas decorated with cempasúchil, a bright orange flower. Pan de muerto is the bread of the season.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: a friendly word for customers, like dear
What can we get you, dear?

cards.note: Sellers use mi reina or mi rey warmly with their customers.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: A local way to say la casa.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: The main meal of the day is eaten between two and four in the afternoon. In the fondas it often comes as a comida corrida.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: When you walk into a place where someone is eating, people say buen provecho. It is a polite wish for a good meal.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Mezcal is sipped slowly, in little sorbitos. It is served with orange and sal de gusano, a salt made with worm.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: People buy pan de yema to dip in chocolate de agua. Bread and chocolate go together here.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: The Guelaguetza takes place in July. It brings dances from the eight regions of Oaxaca.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Día de Muertos is marked with altars, cempasúchil flowers and comparsas, the festive parades.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: My neighbor is from this city.

cards.note: Tapatío is for a man, tapatía for a woman. Both name a person from this city.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: I have no money on me.

cards.note: Lana literally means wool, but in everyday talk it means money.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: A polite way to ask someone to repeat themselves, or to answer when someone calls you.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Here padre means great or cool. It is friendly, everyday talk.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Comida corrida is a set lunch served in the afternoon, usually between 2 and 4 pm.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: People say buen provecho to those who are eating. It is a small, friendly wish for a good meal.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Among friends and family, a greeting is often a kiss on the cheek.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Shop owners greet customers as they walk in, with a buenos días or a buenas tardes.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: Pardon? I didn't hear you well.

cards.note: A polite way to say pardon or yes when someone speaks to you or calls you. It sounds courteous and warm.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Said when you step past someone or want to come in.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: A warm invitation to come in, often said twice.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: People here say provecho to anyone who is eating when you walk in or out of a place. It is a small wish that they enjoy their meal.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: The main meal of the day is the comida corrida, eaten in the afternoon, usually around 2 pm.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In a shop or a fonda, people greet everyone with buenas tardes before asking for anything.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: La Alborada takes place in September. Fireworks light up the sky to honour San Miguel Arcángel.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: The Los Locos parade takes place in June. There are costumes and dancing, and sweets are thrown to the crowd.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: There's a lot of work today.

cards.note: A local word for work, heard in Puebla.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: In Puebla, patrón and jefa are friendly ways to address someone you don't know.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: I'm on my way over soon.

cards.note: In Puebla it means you'll be there soon, though maybe not.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Comida, the main meal, is eaten between 2 and 4 pm. Often it is a menú del día at a fonda, followed by a long sobremesa.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Chiles en nogada are a seasonal dish, eaten in August and September. They come in the colours of the Mexican flag.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Cemitas are eaten standing up at market stalls, usually at lunchtime.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Cinco de Mayo is a local holiday. A big parade commemorates the battle of 1862.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: When you enter a small shop, people greet the owner with "buenas tardes".

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: It comes from callejón, an alley. The verb means to stroll through the narrow streets with no hurry.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: Pardon? I didn't hear you well.

cards.note: A polite way to ask someone to repeat themselves, or to answer when someone calls you.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: What a cool hat you have!

cards.note: Casual slang you hear among friends and people your own age.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: You say it when something surprises you, as a short way to ask "really?"

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In the evenings there are callejoneadas with the estudiantinas. These are groups of students who play music, and people follow them as they stroll through the alleys.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Tunnels run under the city, and people use them to go everywhere. They travel through them by bus, by taxi or on foot.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Every October the town holds the Festival Internacional Cervantino, an international festival.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: For the Day of the Dead, families build altars and visit the cemetery.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: I'm a jarocho, from the port.

cards.note: Jarocha is the form for a woman.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: my love, said by a vendor
What can I give you, love?

cards.note: A vendor may say it to anyone.

cards.headline: At the Café de la Parroquia
cards.note: At the Café de la Parroquia, you tap your glass with a spoon to ask for milk.

cards.headline: Danzón in the evening
cards.note: In the evening, people dance danzón in the zócalo.

cards.headline: Fandangos
cards.note: At a fandango, the music is son jarocho, and anyone can sing a verse.

cards.headline: Carnival
cards.note: Before Lent comes the Carnival, with parades on the malecón.

cards.headline: Buen provecho
cards.note: People say buen provecho to people who are eating.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: Vasco de Quiroga, said with affection

cards.note: Tata comes from Purépecha and is a word of respect for an elder. Vasco de Quiroga is lovingly called Tata Vasco.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: For the Day of the Dead, people keep an all-night vigil on Janitzio. It is one of the best-known customs of the lake.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Each lake town has its own craft, a tradition that goes back to Tata Vasco. The craft each town is known for is part of its identity.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: It is a custom to say buen provecho to people who are eating, even when you do not know them.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Bring a jacket. The evenings are cold by the lake, so people dress warmly once the sun goes down.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Market day is centered around the Plaza Chica. It is a regular part of life in town, and a place where people gather.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: At fiestas, people perform the Danza de los Viejitos. It is a traditional dance that belongs to local celebrations.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Local food includes pescado blanco, corundas, uchepos, sopa tarasca and churipo. They are all part of the regional table.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Maya words like this one turn up in everyday Spanish here.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: the call before a rhyming verse

cards.note: At a vaquería, someone calls it out before a rhyming verse.

rows.en: the last drop left in a glass
Only the last drop is left.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Mi reina is for a woman, mi rey for a man.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: People here often dress in white: the guayabera for men, and the hipil or terno for women.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: People here go out in the evening, once the heat drops.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Sleeping in a hammock is a custom here.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Tsotsil is one of the languages many families here speak at home, so this is how you thank someone in it.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Coleto is for a man and coleta for a woman. It is what people from San Cristóbal call themselves.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: In Chiapas you hear vos used alongside tú. Both mean you.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Use chulo for a masculine word and chula for a feminine one.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Ask before you take anyone's photo here. Never take photos inside the church at Chamula.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Each barrio, or neighborhood, has its own church and its own saint's day. So the town has many local celebrations through the year.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In the evening there is marimba music in the plaza. The town is cold at night, so wear a jacket when you go out.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Many families here speak Tsotsil or Tseltal at home, and Spanish in town.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: People check the wait at la línea before crossing to work, study or shop.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.text: Voy al otro lado a trabajar.
rows.en: I'm going to the other side to work.

cards.note: Literally "the other side." People cross al otro lado to work, study or shop.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: A local way to say yes or OK.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: A local way to say let's go.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Tacos are eaten even after midnight here. Favorites include carne asada with guacamole, adobada, and fish tacos in the Baja style.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In Plaza Santa Cecilia you can hire musicians by the song. You pay for one song at a time, rather than for a whole set.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: On Sundays, people come to dance in Parque Teniente Guerrero.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Here you can pay in pesos or in dollars.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: Excuse me, can you tell me the time?

cards.note: You can use it politely with anyone to get their attention.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.text: Mi tío ya llegó del norte.
rows.en: My uncle just got back from the US.

cards.note: A quick reaction of surprise when someone tells you news.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: Pardon? I didn't hear you well.

cards.note: A polite way to ask someone to say it again.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.text: Mi hermano vive en el otro lado.
rows.en: My brother lives in the United States.

cards.note: Both phrases name the United States in everyday talk.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: A callejoneada is a walk through the alleys behind a tamborazo. A donkey goes along carrying the mezcal.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Mezcal is drunk neat and slowly, a little at a time, not in a rush.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Queso de tuna is a sweet made from cactus fruit. Despite the name, it is a candy, not a cheese.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In December, relatives who live in the United States come home. It is a time when families gather again.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Regio is the word for a man from here, regia for a woman.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: People here say ey for yes.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: People here say ira when they want you to look.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: My uncle is very tight with money.

cards.note: Codo describes someone who hates to spend.

cards.headline: Culture: the weekend grill
cards.note: Weekends are for carne asada, grilled beef shared with the whole family and the neighbours.

cards.headline: Culture: the evening walk
cards.note: When the heat breaks, people go out to walk the Paseo Santa Lucía.

cards.headline: Culture: a December feast
cards.note: On 18 December comes the feast of the Virgen del Roble. Roble means oak, so she is the Virgin of the Oak.

cards.headline: Culture: a local sweet
cards.note: Glorias are a sweet made of milk and pecan. They come from Linares.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: I'm a patasalada, I was born here.

cards.note: Literally "salty foot", it is a local name for a person from here.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: Shall we go to the beach, guys?

cards.note: Depending on who is talking, plebes can mean kids, guys or friends.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: A short, local way to say yes.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: A local way to say something is cool.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Carnival falls in the week before Lent. Parades fill the malecón, the seaside promenade.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Winter is baseball season, and the local team is the Venados.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: On the beach you can hire a banda, a band, to play for you. You pay by the song.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: Café de olla is made in a clay pot with cinnamon and piloncillo, which is unrefined cane sugar.

cards.headline: About this market stall
cards.note: Here a quesadilla doesn't automatically come with cheese; it's "con queso" only if you ask. Huitlacoche, a common filling, is a prized fungus that grows on corn.

cards.headline: About this taquería
cards.note: Tacos al pastor are cut straight off the trompo, with a bit of pineapple on top. You order standing at the counter and say "con todo".

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: This cathedral, the largest in Latin America, stands on soft lake-bed clay over part of the old Aztec ceremonial precinct. It has sunk unevenly, and plumb lines hang inside.

cards.headline: About this cantina
cards.note: Opened in 1895, this cantina still has its carved wooden bar, tall mirrors and ornate ceiling. A bullet hole in the ceiling is said to be Pancho Villa's, though nobody can prove it.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The Alameda is the oldest public park in the Americas, laid out in 1592 and named for its álamos, the poplar trees.

cards.headline: About this churrería
cards.note: El Moro has been open day and night since 1935. The hot chocolate comes light, called mexicano, or thick, called español.

cards.headline: About this street food
cards.note: Tricycle vendors sell tamales verdes, rojos, de rajas and de dulce, with atole to drink. The guajolota is a tamal inside a bolillo.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: A tlayuda is a large, crisp corn tortilla spread with asiento (pork lard), beans and quesillo. Tasajo and cecina enchilada are grilled over charcoal in the aisle, so smoke fills the market.

cards.headline: About this mezcalería
cards.note: Mezcal is served in small copitas and sipped slowly with orange slices and sal de gusano, ground dried agave worm with salt and chile. Espadín is the agave most often poured.

cards.headline: About this fonda
cards.note: This is the land of seven moles: negro, coloradito, amarillo, rojo, verde, chichilo and manchamanteles. Mole negro gets its dark color from chiles chilhuacles and toasted seeds, and takes days to make.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: This is one of the city's oldest barrios, with a Nahuatl name. When it holds a fiesta, bells and cohetes announce it from morning, and a calenda procession with puppets winds through the streets.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: At sunset everyone strolls here and along the pedestrian street that leads to Santo Domingo. The plaza is lined with arcades full of cafés and restaurants, with the Catedral on its north side.

cards.headline: About this garden
cards.note: The garden can only be visited with a guide. It grows on land that belonged to the Santo Domingo monastery. Cochineal, the insect behind the red dye, lives on nopal cacti.

cards.headline: About this archaeological site
cards.note: This is a Zapotec city built on a levelled mountaintop more than two thousand years ago. Its Gran Plaza is a vast levelled square with temples along its sides. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.headline: About this market stall
cards.note: Tejuino is a cold drink of fermented corn masa and piloncillo, served with lime, salt and ice. It is typical of Jalisco. Many people order it with a scoop of lime nieve on top.

cards.headline: About this cantina
cards.note: Tequila is made from blue agave in Jalisco. In a traditional cantina it comes in a small caballito, often with sangrita on the side, a Jalisco invention, while botanas fill the table to share.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: The Colonia Americana was built in the early 20th century. Its houses copy American and European styles, hence the name. Avenida Chapultepec, its main street, has a wide tree-lined walkway down the middle.

cards.headline: About this bakery
cards.note: Birote salado is the crusty sourdough roll Guadalajara is known for. It is the only bread that works for tortas ahogadas, so people come early, before it sells out.

cards.headline: About this workshop
cards.note: Tlaquepaque is known for its pottery. Barro bruñido is a local style in which the clay surface is polished by hand with a smooth stone. Handmade pieces are never perfectly uniform.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The Hospicio Cabañas was an orphanage. Orozco's mural Man of Fire is in its dome, and children often lie on the benches below to look up at it.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Mariachi comes from Jalisco. A group has violins, trumpets, a guitarrón and a vihuela, and the players wear the charro suit. Groups wait here to be hired for a song, a birthday or a serenade.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: The market is named after Ignacio Ramírez, known as "El Nigromante", who was born in this town. Stalls here sell flowers for the church and for the altar at home.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: In the evening the Jardín fills for the paseo, with families, couples and mariachis.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The Parroquia's pink-stone neo-Gothic façade was designed in the late 1800s by Zeferino Gutiérrez, a local self-taught builder. The church faces the Jardín, the town's main square.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: Café de olla is brewed in a clay pot with piloncillo and cinnamon. A concha or a pan de nata goes with it.

cards.headline: About this art centre
cards.note: Fábrica La Aurora was a textile mill until it closed in the 1990s. Now it is an art and design centre of studios and galleries, and visitors can walk in.

cards.headline: About this taquería
cards.note: For tacos al pastor, the pork turns on a vertical spit called a trompo, with a pineapple on top. The method comes from the shawarma brought to Mexico by Lebanese immigrants.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: Ignacio Allende was born in 1769 in the house on the Jardín, now a museum. In 1810 he and Father Hidalgo started the fight for independence.

cards.headline: About this candy shop
cards.note: On Calle 6 Oriente, the "Calle de los Dulces", people buy sweets to take home as gifts. Tortitas de Santa Clara are made of pumpkin-seed paste and named after Puebla's Santa Clara convent.

cards.headline: About this fonda
cards.note: Chiles en nogada come in late summer, when walnuts and pomegranates are fresh. Their green, white and red match the Mexican flag.

cards.headline: About this library
cards.note: It began in 1646, when Bishop Juan de Palafox gave his books to the seminary on condition that anyone could read them. Poblanos call it the first public library in the Americas.

cards.headline: About this barrio
cards.note: Xanenetla is one of the oldest barrios of Puebla. Its murals cover the neighbours' own house fronts, painted together with the people who live behind them.

cards.headline: About this cantina
cards.note: La Pasita is known for its pasita, a raisin liqueur. It's served in a small glass with a raisin, a bit of cheese and a toothpick.

cards.headline: About this taquería
cards.note: Tacos árabes are the favorite late-night street food in Puebla, so taquerías like this are busiest at night.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The Templo de Santo Domingo is one of the best-known churches in the Centro Histórico, famous for its richly decorated Capilla del Rosario.

cards.headline: About this street
cards.note: After floods the river was diverted. Its old bed, under old stone bridges, became tunnels that now carry most of the traffic. The callejones above are too narrow and steep for cars.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The Count of Valenciana built this church, with carved altars covered in gold. The Valenciana mine next door was one of the richest silver mines in the world.

cards.headline: About this fonda
cards.note: Enchiladas mineras: tortillas dipped in guajillo chile sauce, filled with cheese and onion, covered with fried potatoes and carrots. They are said to have been the miners' food, cheap and filling.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: This was a grain store where the Spanish took refuge in 1810, in the first great battle of the War of Independence. Today a regional museum, its stairway murals painted from the 1950s.

cards.headline: About this theatre
cards.note: This grand theatre was opened in 1903 by President Porfirio Díaz. Inside, it is all red velvet and gilded Moorish decoration.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: This café goes back to the early 1800s. The famous order is the lechero: strong coffee in a glass. Tap it with a spoon and a waiter pours hot milk from high up.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Couples dance danzón here in the open air several evenings a week, to a live band. Danzón came from Cuba in the late 1800s and this city made it its own.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: This is the last bastion left of the walls that surrounded the city. It was built in the seventeenth century against pirates; the rest of the wall was pulled down as the city grew.

cards.headline: About this pier
cards.note: The catch here is often huachinango, red snapper. Coast cooks make it a la veracruzana, with tomato, olives, capers and pickled chiles, and the riverside restaurants buy straight from the boats.

cards.headline: About this food stall
cards.note: Picadas are the breakfast of the port: thick rounds of corn dough with pinched edges, topped with red or green salsa, cheese and onion. Gordas are small fat tortillas.

cards.headline: About this cemetery
cards.note: On the night of 1 November, Purépecha families on Janitzio keep vigil here with candles, cempasúchil flowers, bread and the dead person's favourite food, welcoming the souls who return.

cards.headline: About this fonda
cards.note: Here the food of the lake is sopa tarasca, a bean and tomato soup with fried tortilla strips and chile, and corundas, triangular tamales eaten with cream and salsa.

cards.headline: About this workshop
cards.note: Pátzcuaro's maque, or lacquer, is often black, painted with flowers and birds and outlined in fine gold leaf. The craft predates the Spanish, and a single tray takes many layers and many days.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Named for Vasco de Quiroga, first bishop of Michoacán, still called Tata Vasco. He is credited with giving each Purépecha lake town a craft: copper, pottery, guitars, lacquer. Many still do.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Tzintzuntzan was the capital of the Purépecha kingdom before the Spanish came. Its five yácatas are pyramids with a round part and a rectangular part, unlike any others in Mexico.

cards.headline: About this park
cards.note: Trova yucateca is romantic song for two guitars and voices, sung here in a serenata since the 1960s. The park has confidentes: white S-shaped seats where two people sit facing each other.

cards.headline: About this boulevard
cards.note: This boulevard was modeled on the Paris boulevards. Its mansions were built with henequen money, the "green gold" of Yucatán; now some are museums, banks and hotels.

cards.headline: About this kibi counter
cards.note: A kibi is the Arab kibbeh of ground meat and wheat, brought by Lebanese families in the late nineteenth century. Here it is fried and eaten with pickled red onion and habanero.

cards.headline: About this chapel
cards.note: This small eighteenth-century chapel is also called the chapel of the good journey. Travellers leaving on the royal road used to stop here to pray for a safe trip.

cards.headline: About this workshop
cards.note: Many Yucatecans sleep in a hammock rather than a bed, because it is cooler, and every house has hooks in the walls. A good hammock takes weeks to weave.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Inside this church there are no pews and no regular Mass. The floor is covered with pine needles, and families kneel among candles to pray in Tsotsil. Photographs inside are strictly forbidden.

cards.headline: About this comedor
cards.note: Tamales here come three Chiapas ways: de chipilín, with a green herb in the dough; de bola, filled with pork, prunes and raisins; and de hoja de plátano, wrapped in banana leaf.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: Chiapas produces more coffee than any other state in Mexico, most of it grown by Indigenous families on small mountain plots, in the shade of taller trees. The cherries are picked red by hand.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Each town of the highlands has its own clothes. In Zinacantán they are covered in embroidered flowers, because the town grows flowers in greenhouses. One blouse can take a month to make.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The marimba is the instrument of Chiapas and a symbol of the state. It is a long wooden keyboard with resonators underneath, played by three or four people at once.

cards.headline: About this restaurant
cards.note: The Caesar salad was born here in the 1920s, when Americans crossed the border during Prohibition. The story goes that Caesar Cardini made it in 1924 from what was left in the kitchen.

cards.headline: About this taquería
cards.note: The local taco is carne asada: beef grilled over mesquite charcoal, on a corn tortilla with onion, cilantro, salsa and guacamole. People here are sure the best tacos in the country are theirs.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: This has been the traditional market since the 1950s. Stalls sell southern foods like chile pasilla, chapulines and quesillo, and Baja California cheese and dates.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The tiled minaret was the chimney of the Agua Caliente casino's boiler house. The casino opened in 1928, when gambling was banned in the United States, and Hollywood crossed the border to play.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Named for the patron saint of musicians, this plaza is where people hire a group by the song or by the hour, for a birthday, a serenade or a funeral: mariachis or norteños.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: This city is built of cantera rosa, a soft pink stone that hardens in the air. The cathedral's front, finished in the mid-1700s, is carved like lace and was paid for by silver found here in 1546.

cards.headline: About this fonda
cards.note: A fonda like this serves gorditas: thick corn tortillas cooked on the comal, split open and filled with stew. The dish of weddings here is asado de boda, pork in a dark red chile sauce.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: This museum, in the ruins of a sixteenth-century convent, holds thousands of Mexican masks, one of the largest collections in the world, carved for village dances: devils, jaguars, Moors and Christians.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: In the last days of August, thousands dress as Moors and Christians on these hills and act out old battles, with drums, bugles and gunpowder. The tradition is about two hundred years old.

cards.headline: About this bus terminal
cards.note: The royal silver road, the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, once ran through here from Mexico City to Santa Fe, New Mexico. Buses still run north and south along it.

cards.headline: About this restaurant
cards.note: Cabrito is the dish of Nuevo León: a milk-fed kid goat, opened flat on an iron stake and cooked for hours beside mesquite embers, never over the flame. Served with flour tortillas.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Horno 3 is a blast furnace from the steelworks founded in 1900, Latin America's first big one. It closed in 1986; the grounds are now a park, and Horno 3 a museum.

cards.headline: About this pier
cards.note: A canal and riverwalk about 2.5 kilometres long, from the Macroplaza to Parque Fundidora. Opened in 2007, it is named for the springs of Santa Lucía, where Monterrey was founded in 1596.

cards.headline: About this street food
cards.note: Tacos mañaneros are small breakfast tacos in flour tortillas, filled with stews. Machacado is sun-dried beef, pounded and scrambled with egg; drying was how the north kept meat in the desert heat.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The Virgen del Roble is the patron of Monterrey. Legend says her image was found in an oak tree and kept returning to it, so a chapel was built. Her feast is 18 December.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The plaza was laid out in the 1830s on land given by Juan Nepomuceno Machado, a merchant of silver, cloth and pearls. It is the heart of the old town.

cards.headline: About this theatre
cards.note: The Teatro Ángela Peralta opened in 1874. It later became a cinema, then a ruin after a hurricane, until the city restored it in 1992. Today it hosts opera, ballet and an autumn festival.

cards.headline: About this lighthouse
cards.note: El Faro stands on a hill that was once an island, about 150 metres above the sea, one of the highest lighthouses in the world. The view covers the whole port.

cards.headline: About this street market
cards.note: The changueras, all women, have sold shrimp from tubs of ice on this street for generations. The whole city buys here, by the kilo and by size, for ceviche, aguachile or the grill.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Each of the cathedral's twenty-eight stained-glass windows has a six-pointed star. People say it thanks a Jewish family of the port who gave money to finish the building.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Parque México follows the oval shape of the old Hipódromo de la Condesa racetrack. It opened in 1927 and sits at the heart of a neighborhood known for its Art Deco buildings.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Work on the Catedral began in 1573 and ended in 1813, so it mixes several styles. It stands on the soft lakebed of old Lake Texcoco and has sunk unevenly over time.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The Alameda Central was created in 1592 and is one of the oldest public parks in the Americas. Its name comes from the álamos, the poplar trees planted there.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Along the main staircase of the Palacio Nacional, Diego Rivera painted a huge mural of Mexican history, from before the Spanish arrived to the twentieth century. He worked on it from 1929 to 1935.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The Jardín Centenario has a fountain with coyote statues at its center. The name Coyoacán comes from Nahuatl and is usually translated as "place of coyotes."

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Jardín Conzatti is named for Cassiano Conzatti, an Italian-born botanist who worked in Oaxaca and studied its plants. It is a small, tree-shaded plaza in the city centre.

cards.headline: About this garden
cards.note: The Jardín Etnobotánico grows plants of Oaxaca, beside the Santo Domingo church and former monastery. You visit on a guided tour, which explains the plants and how people have used them.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The Zócalo is the main square of Oaxaca. The cathedral and the Palacio de Gobierno face each other across it, and arcades with cafés and restaurants run along its edges.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Monte Albán was a great Zapotec capital, founded around 500 BC on a levelled mountaintop above the valleys. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site, listed together with Oaxaca's historic centre.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The Hospicio Cabañas began as an orphanage and hospice in the early 1800s. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site, famous for José Clemente Orozco's murals, including the Man of Fire in the dome.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Mariachi music comes from Jalisco. In this plaza, mariachi bands wait in their suits to be hired, to play a few songs for a birthday, a serenade or a party.

cards.headline: About this market stall
cards.note: The market is named for Ignacio Ramírez, known as El Nigromante, a writer and liberal thinker born in San Miguel in 1818.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The Jardín is the town's main square, right in front of the parish church. Its laurel trees are trimmed into tidy rounded shapes, and people meet on its benches.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Its pink stone Gothic-style façade dates from the late 1800s, built by Zeferino Gutiérrez, a local self-taught mason. He is said to have drawn on postcards of European churches.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: This was the birthplace of Ignacio Allende, a leader of Mexico's independence movement. The town's name honors him, and his family home is now a museum.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: El Mirador is a lookout above the town. From here you can see the spires of the parish church and the rooftops of the center spread out below.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Its Rosary Chapel, finished in 1690, is covered in gold leaf from floor to ceiling. It is one of the finest examples of Mexican baroque, and people often call it a wonder.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The zócalo is the main square. The cathedral stands on one side, and arcades called portales run along the others, lined with cafés and restaurants where people sit and watch the day go by.

cards.headline: About this library
cards.note: Bishop Juan de Palafox founded it in 1646 and gave his books for public use. It is often called the first public library in the Americas, and its shelves still hold old books.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: This small triangular garden is the city's living room. Trimmed laurel trees shade the benches, and there is a bandstand in the middle. People meet here to sit, talk and listen to music.

cards.headline: About this theater
cards.note: Opened in 1903 and named for President Benito Juárez, this theater has a richly decorated, Moorish-inspired interior. It is one of the main stages of the Festival Internacional Cervantino.

cards.headline: About this monument
cards.note: The statue honors El Pípila, a miner credited with a daring act in 1810 during the fight for independence. It stands high above the city, so the view of the colorful hillside houses is the reason to climb.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: It was built as a grain storehouse. In 1810, early in Mexico's war of independence, it became the site of a major battle. Today the building holds a museum of the region's history.

cards.headline: About this university
cards.note: The University of Guanajuato traces its roots to a Jesuit school founded in 1732. Its students are a big part of everyday life in the city's streets and plazas.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Built in the late 1700s with money from the owner of the nearby Valenciana silver mine, this church is famous for its ornate baroque front and its gold-covered altarpieces inside.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: This house is where the painter Diego Rivera was born in 1886. Today it is a museum with some of his artwork and furniture from the family's home.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The main square is lined with arcades full of cafés, with the Palacio Municipal on one side and the Parroquia de la Asunción on another. Musicians often play here in the evenings.

cards.headline: About this fort
cards.note: Spain built this fortress on a reef to guard the harbor from pirates. It later served as a prison, and Spanish troops held it until 1825.

cards.headline: About this bulwark
cards.note: This is the only surviving bastion of the wall that once ringed the town. It was built in the 1600s to defend against pirate attacks.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: This museum honors Agustín Lara, the songwriter behind "Solamente una vez" and "Granada", one of Mexico's best-loved composers.

cards.headline: About this cemetery
cards.note: On the night of Day of the Dead, families keep vigil at the graves here with candles, marigolds and food for their dead. It is one of the best-known places in Mexico for this custom.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The plaza is named for Vasco de Quiroga, a 16th-century bishop who helped nearby Purépecha villages each develop their own craft. A monument to him stands in the middle.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The Virgin of Health inside is made from a paste of corn stalks, a craft technique of the Purépecha people. Pilgrims come to ask her for healing.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The yácatas are large stone platforms with a rounded side and a rectangular side. They were the ceremonial center of the Purépecha capital before the Spanish arrived.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Santa Lucía is a small plaza with arcades, beside a church. It is known for its weekly serenata: an evening of Yucatecan trova music, song and traditional dance, open to anyone who wants to listen.

cards.headline: About this palace
cards.note: This palace is the seat of the state government. Its staircase and walls are covered with large murals by Fernando Castro Pacheco that tell the story of the Maya and of Yucatán.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: This museum is devoted to Maya culture, ancient and living. Its building is modeled on the ceiba, the sacred tree of the Maya, and inside are many artifacts from across the Maya world.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: An ermita is a small chapel. This one dates from the 1700s, and travelers setting out on a long road used to stop here to pray for a safe journey.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Inside, there are no pews. The floor is covered in pine needles and candles, and families kneel to pray in Tsotsil, often with offerings. Photos are not allowed.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Next to the Santo Domingo church, artisans sell hand-woven textiles from nearby Maya communities, along with amber jewelry.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: This is the main square. It is named for March 31, 1528, the date the city was founded. The cathedral faces it.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The church stands on a small hill, reached by a long flight of steps. Each December 12, the feast of the Virgin of Guadalupe, people gather here to celebrate.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: This was the home of archaeologist Frans Blom and photographer Gertrude Duby Blom, who worked with the Lacandón Maya. Na Bolom means "House of the Jaguar" in Tsotsil.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Its baroque front is painted ochre and red and carved with figures. Building began in the 1500s.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Plaza Santa Cecilia is known as the mariachi plaza. Musicians in charro suits wait here to be hired for a song. Santa Cecilia is the patron saint of musicians.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The minaret is a reminder of the Agua Caliente resort, which opened in 1928. Its casino and hotel drew Americans and Hollywood stars across the border during Prohibition.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The cathedral's front is carved from pink quarry stone in the Baroque style. It was built in the 1700s and is one of the finest examples of Mexican Baroque.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: This hill towers over the city. In 1914 Pancho Villa's army won a decisive battle against federal troops here, a turning point of the Mexican Revolution. Today a cable car carries visitors up.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: The museum sits inside the ruins of a 16th-century convent. It is known for its huge collection of Mexican masks, many used in traditional dances and festivals.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: This is the heart of the old town. The carved front of the cathedral rises over it, and the state government palace stands nearby, so people gather here to meet and stroll.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Opened in 1984, this chain of plazas and gardens covers about 40 hectares, often called one of the largest city plazas anywhere. The orange Faro del Comercio, by Luis Barragán, shines a green laser at night.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Horno 3 is a blast furnace from the Fundidora steel foundry, which closed in 1986. Today the old furnace is a museum about steel, so you can walk inside where molten iron was once made.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: This hilltop building was finished in the 1780s as a bishop's residence. In 1846 it served as a fort during the Battle of Monterrey. Today it is the regional museum of Nuevo León.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: A small square ringed by restored 19th-century buildings. Cafés and restaurants set their tables out under the open sky, so it is where the historic center gathers to eat, talk and listen to music.

cards.headline: About this theater
cards.note: It opened in 1874 and was later renamed for Ángela Peralta, the singer called the Mexican Nightingale. She sang here in 1883, shortly before she died of yellow fever. It was restored and reopened in 1992.

cards.headline: About this lighthouse
cards.note: It stands on a natural hill about 150 metres above the sea. It is counted among the highest natural-hill lighthouses in the world, and ships out at sea can see its light from far away.

cards.headline: About this cathedral
cards.note: Work began in the 1850s and ended near the close of the 19th century. It mixes several architectural styles, and its two tall towers and golden-yellow stonework make it easy to spot.

cards.headline: This or that
cards.note: Buenas on its own is a short hello. Buenas noches works for hello and goodbye after dark.

cards.headline: This or that

rows.en: Sure, that works, see you then.

cards.note: Sale and va are both everyday Mexican ways to say OK to a plan.

cards.headline: This or that

rows.en: This one, the one near me.
That one, near you or a bit away.

cards.note: Aquel is for something far away.

cards.headline: This or that
cards.note: Mexicans say en la mañana where Spain says por la mañana.

cards.headline: This or that
cards.note: Acá and allá are common in Mexico.

cards.headline: This or that
cards.note: Con and sin go straight before the food: con todo, sin cebolla.

cards.headline: This or that
cards.note: Travel by vehicle uses en: en metro, en camión.

cards.headline: This or that
cards.note: Words that describe a thing usually come after it: salsa verde, agua natural.

cards.headline: This or that

rows.en: How much shall I give you?

rows.text: Medio kilo de tomate, por favor.
rows.en: Half a kilo of tomatoes, please.

rows.text: Un kilo de tomate, por favor.

cards.note: Weights and portions link to the food with de: un cuarto de, doscientos gramos de.

cards.headline: This or that

rows.text: Un agua de jamaica, por favor.
Un agua de horchata, por favor.

cards.note: De plus a second word names the flavour or filling: tacos de pastor, agua de jamaica.

cards.headline: This or that
cards.note: In Mexico planta baja is the ground floor and primer piso is one floor up.

cards.headline: This or that
cards.note: Clock times always take la or las: a la una, a las cinco.

cards.headline: This or that
cards.note: After antes de and después de, the verb stays in its look-up form: comer.

cards.headline: This or that
cards.note: Place phrases end in de: enfrente de, al lado de, cerca de, lejos de.

cards.headline: This or that
cards.note: A says how far: a dos cuadras, a cinco minutos.

cards.headline: This or that
cards.note: Bueno and malo lose their -o before tiempo: buen tiempo, mal tiempo.

cards.headline: This or that
cards.note: Bien before a describing word makes it stronger, like muy: bien dulces, bien rico.

cards.headline: This or that

rows.en: Wait a little bit for me, please.

cards.note: Tantito means a little bit and softens a request. The -ito in momentito makes a word kinder.

cards.headline: This or that

rows.en: How much sugar do you want?

cards.note: Mucho and poco change to match the thing: mucha azúcar, poca gente.

cards.headline: This or that

rows.en: I went the day before yesterday.

cards.note: Antier is the Mexican word for the day before yesterday.

cards.headline: This or that
cards.note: After a no me gusta, you agree with a mí tampoco and disagree with a mí sí.

cards.headline: This or that

rows.text: ¿Se lleva el vestido o la falda?
rows.en: Are you taking the dress or the skirt?

cards.note: Me lo llevo and me la llevo both mean I'll take it. Lo or la matches what you're buying.

cards.headline: This or that
cards.note: El and la can stand for a thing already mentioned: el de allá, la roja.

cards.headline: This or that
cards.note: Seguido is the everyday Mexican word for often.

cards.headline: Two places: a famous mole

rows.en: Oaxaca: I want to try the mole negro.
Puebla: I want to try the mole poblano.

cards.note: Mole is a rich sauce served over meat. Each of these cities is proud of its own.

cards.headline: Two places: a corn drink

rows.en: Oaxaca: a cold corn and cacao drink.
Guadalajara: a cold fermented corn drink.

cards.note: Both are cold drinks made from corn, but each belongs to its own region.

cards.headline: Two places: a famous spirit

rows.en: Oaxaca: I want to try a mezcal.
Guadalajara: I want to try a tequila.

cards.note: Oaxaca is famous for mezcal. Guadalajara is in Jalisco, the home state of tequila.

cards.headline: Two places: a famous roast
cards.note: Cochinita pibil is pork slow-cooked with achiote. Cabrito is young goat, roasted.

cards.headline: Two places: saying thank you

rows.en: San Cristóbal: thank you, in Tsotsil.
Mérida: thank you, in Yucatec Maya.

cards.note: Both are Maya languages, spoken at home by many people in these two places.

cards.headline: Two places: a street-food sandwich

rows.en: Mexico City: a tamal in a roll, please.
Guadalajara: a roll drowned in sauce.

cards.note: A guajolota is a tamal inside a bread roll. A torta ahogada is a pork roll soaked in chile sauce.

cards.headline: Two places: a seafood dish

rows.en: Veracruz: fish in tomato and olive sauce.
Mazatlán: raw shrimp in chile and lime.

cards.note: The coast gives both, but the cooking is very different.

rows.en: Oaxaca: a big crisp tortilla with toppings.
Mérida: fried tortillas stuffed with beans.

rows.text: Unos chiles en nogada, por favor.
rows.en: Puebla: stuffed chiles in walnut sauce.
